claim: CRF1 receptors are critical to stress responses because they allow neurons to respond to CRF released in response to stress.
source: Corticotropin-releasing factor type-1 (CRF1) receptors are critical to stress responses because they allow neurons to respond to CRF released in response to stress.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about CRF1 receptor function in stress responses.

claim: Crhr1 and Cre mRNA expression are highly colocalized in both the central amygdala (CeA) and in the basolateral amygdala (BLA).
source: We report that Crhr1 and Cre mRNA expression are highly colocalized in both the central amygdala (CeA), composed of mostly GABAergic neurons, and in the basolateral amygdala (BLA), composed of mostly glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript showing >90% colocalization in CeA and >98% in BLA.

claim: In the CeA, membrane properties, inhibitory synaptic transmission, and responses to CRF bath application in tdTomato+ neurons are similar to those previously reported in GFP+ cells in CRFR1-GFP mice.
source: In the CeA, membrane properties, inhibitory synaptic transmission, and responses to CRF bath application in tdTomato+ neurons are similar to those previously reported in GFP+ cells in CRFR1-GFP mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data from the manuscript and comparison to published literature on CRFR1-GFP mice.

claim: Stimulatory DREADD receptors can be targeted to CeA CRF1+ cells via virally delivered Cre-dependent transgenes.
source: We show that stimulatory DREADD receptors can be targeted to CeA CRF1+ cells via virally delivered Cre-dependent transgenes, that transfected Cre/tdTomato+ cells are activated by clozapine-n-oxide in vitro and in vivo
evidence: This is demonstrated by viral injection experiments and subsequent validation through c-Fos immunohistochemistry and electrophysiology.

claim: Transfected Cre/tdTomato+ cells are activated by clozapine-n-oxide in vitro and in vivo.
source: We show that stimulatory DREADD receptors can be targeted to CeA CRF1+ cells via virally delivered Cre-dependent transgenes, that transfected Cre/tdTomato+ cells are activated by clozapine-n-oxide in vitro and in vivo
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data showing CNO-induced depolarization and firing, and c-Fos immunohistochemistry showing increased c-Fos expression after CNO treatment.

claim: Activation of CeA CRF1+ cells in vivo increases anxiety-like and nocifensive behaviors.
source: that activation of these cells in vivo increases anxiety-like and nocifensive behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from EPM, open field, and Von Frey tests following DREADD-mediated activation of CeA CRF1+ cells.

claim: Cre-tdTomato is expressed in several brain areas across the brain.
source: Outside the amygdala, we show that Cre-tdTomato is expressed in several brain areas across the brain
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence imaging of coronal sections across the rostrocaudal axis showing tdTomato expression in multiple brain regions.

claim: The expression pattern of Cre-tdTomato cells is similar to the known expression pattern of CRF1 cells.
source: and that the expression pattern of Cre-tdTomato cells is similar to the known expression pattern of CRF1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of tdTomato expression patterns with published reports of Crhr1 mRNA expression in wildtype rats and CRF1-GFP expression in mice.

claim: CRF is a 41 amino acid neuropeptide that acts on various cell populations in the brain and elicits stress-related behavioral and physiological responses.
source: Corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) is a 41 amino acid neuropeptide that acts on various cell populations in the brain and elicits stress-related behavioral (e.g. anxiety) and physiological (e.g. sympathomimetic) responses (Vale et al., 1981; Henckens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRF supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CRF released by neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) into the hypophyseal portal system stimulates adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) release from the pituitary.
source: In the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, CRF released by neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) into the hypophyseal portal system stimulates adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) release from the pituitary, which in turn stimulates release of glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of the HPA axis.

claim: ACTH release from the pituitary stimulates release of glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex.
source: In the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, CRF released by neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) into the hypophyseal portal system stimulates adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) release from the pituitary, which in turn stimulates release of glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of the HPA axis.

claim: Glucocorticoids released into the circulatory system serve as effectors of the HPA axis by modulating various physiological functions.
source: Glucocorticoids released into the circulatory system serve as effectors of the HPA axis by modulating various physiological (e.g. cardiovascular, respiratory, and immune) functions (Smith and Vale, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about glucocorticoid function supported by citation.

claim: Extrahypothalamic CRF neurons are located in many brain areas that modulate affective states and behaviors, such as the amygdala, cortex, hippocampus, midbrain, and locus coeruleus.
source: Extrahypothalamic CRF neurons are located in many brain areas that modulate affective states and behaviors, such as the amygdala, cortex, hippocampus, midbrain, and locus coeruleus (Peng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRF neuron distribution supported by citation.

claim: The extended amygdala, particularly the central amygdala (CeA) and bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST), contain the highest densities of CRF neurons.
source: Among these brain areas, the extended amygdala, particularly the central amygdala (CeA) and bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST), contain the highest densities of CRF neurons (Peng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRF neuron density supported by citation.

claim: CRF type-1 (CRF1) receptors are Gs- or Gq-coupled metabotropic receptors.
source: CRF type-1 (CRF1) receptors are Gs- or Gq-coupled metabotropic receptors (Milan-Lobo et al., 2009; Wanat et al., 2008)
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRF1 receptor signaling supported by citations.

claim: CRF1 receptors are highly expressed in brain areas that contain high densities of CRF fibers and/or CRF neurons, including the CeA, BNST, and medial amygdala.
source: that are highly expressed in brain areas that contain high densities of CRF fibers and/or CRF neurons, including the CeA, BNST, and medial amygdala.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRF1 receptor distribution.

claim: CRF signaling via CRF1 modulates neurophysiological processes underlying stress reactivity, anxiety-related behaviors, learning and memory processes including fear acquisition and/or expression, pain signaling, and addiction-related behaviors.
source: CRF signaling via CRF1 modulates neurophysiological processes underlying stress reactivity, anxiety-related behaviors, learning and memory processes including fear acquisition and/or expression, pain signaling, and addiction-related behaviors (see reviews by Dedic et al., 2018; Henckens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRF1 function supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The central amygdala (CeA) is a key nucleus in modulating affective states and behaviors related to stress, anxiety, fear, pain, and addiction.
source: The central amygdala (CeA) is a key nucleus in modulating affective states and behaviors related to stress, anxiety, fear, pain, and addiction (Gilpin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CeA function supported by citation.

claim: The CeA serves as a major output nucleus of the amygdala.
source: Functionally, the CeA serves as a major output nucleus of the amygdala and can be anatomically divided into lateral (CeAl) and medial (CeAm) subdivisions (Duvarci and Pare, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CeA anatomy and function supported by citation.

claim: The CeA can be anatomically divided into lateral (CeAl) and medial (CeAm) subdivisions.
source: Functionally, the CeA serves as a major output nucleus of the amygdala and can be anatomically divided into lateral (CeAl) and medial (CeAm) subdivisions (Duvarci and Pare, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CeA anatomy supported by citation.

claim: In mice and rats, CRF-expressing (CRF+) neurons are densely localized to the CeAl.
source: In mice and rats, CRF-expressing (CRF+) neurons are densely localized to the CeAl, whereas CRF1-expressing (CRF1+) neurons are mostly localized to the CeAm (Day et al., 1999; Jolkkonen and Pitkänen, 1998; Justice et al., 2008; Pomrenze et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRF neuron distribution supported by multiple citations.

claim: In mice and rats, CRF1-expressing (CRF1+) neurons are mostly localized to the CeAm.
source: In mice and rats, CRF-expressing (CRF+) neurons are densely localized to the CeAl, whereas CRF1-expressing (CRF1+) neurons are mostly localized to the CeAm (Day et al., 1999; Jolkkonen and Pitkänen, 1998; Justice et al., 2008; Pomrenze et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRF1 neuron distribution supported by multiple citations.

claim: The CeAm receives CRF inputs from the bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST).
source: In addition to receiving CRF input from CRF+ neurons in the CeAl, the CeAm receives CRF inputs from distal brain areas such as the bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST) (Dabrowska et al., 2016) and dorsal raphe nucleus (Commons et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CeA connectivity supported by citation.

claim: The CeAm receives CRF inputs from the dorsal raphe nucleus.
source: In addition to receiving CRF input from CRF+ neurons in the CeAl, the CeAm receives CRF inputs from distal brain areas such as the bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST) (Dabrowska et al., 2016) and dorsal raphe nucleus (Commons et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CeA connectivity supported by citation.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of CeA CRF1 attenuates stress-induced increases in anxiety-like behavior.
source: For example, pharmacological blockade of CeA CRF1 attenuates stress-induced increases in anxiety-like behavior (Henry et al., 2006), nociception (Itoga et al., 2016), and alcohol drinking (Roberto et al., 2010; Weera et al., 2020), as well as fear acquisition and expression (Sanford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of CeA CRF1 attenuates stress-induced increases in nociception.
source: For example, pharmacological blockade of CeA CRF1 attenuates stress-induced increases in anxiety-like behavior (Henry et al., 2006), nociception (Itoga et al., 2016), and alcohol drinking (Roberto et al., 2010; Weera et al., 2020), as well as fear acquisition and expression (Sanford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of CeA CRF1 attenuates stress-induced increases in alcohol drinking.
source: For example, pharmacological blockade of CeA CRF1 attenuates stress-induced increases in anxiety-like behavior (Henry et al., 2006), nociception (Itoga et al., 2016), and alcohol drinking (Roberto et al., 2010; Weera et al., 2020), as well as fear acquisition and expression (Sanford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of CeA CRF1 attenuates fear acquisition and expression.
source: For example, pharmacological blockade of CeA CRF1 attenuates stress-induced increases in anxiety-like behavior (Henry et al., 2006), nociception (Itoga et al., 2016), and alcohol drinking (Roberto et al., 2010; Weera et al., 2020), as well as fear acquisition and expression (Sanford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: Mice have a limited behavioral repertoire when compared to rats.
source: However, mice have a limited behavioral repertoire when compared to rats, making the study of more complex behaviors (e.g. drug self-administration and social interaction; Homberg et al., 2017) difficult.
evidence: This is a general statement about species differences in behavioral complexity supported by citation.

claim: The design of the CRF1:Cre rat BAC transgene is similar to the design used to generate CRFR1:Cre BAC transgenic mice.
source: The design of the CRF1:Cre rat BAC transgene is similar to the design used to generate CRFR1:Cre BAC transgenic mice (Jiang et al., 2018), with the exception that a BAC clone from rat was used (clone RNB2-336H12 from Riken Rat genomic BAC library).
evidence: This describes the design strategy used in the current study with reference to a previous mouse study.

claim: The BAC clone used lacks any other identified protein encoding genetic sequences.
source: The BAC clone used lacks any other identified protein encoding genetic sequences, reducing the possibility that other genes will be expressed from BAC when introduced into the rat genome.
evidence: This is a statement about the BAC clone characteristics based on genomic analysis.

claim: iCre is a codon-optimized Cre that produces consistent Cre activity.
source: iCre is a codon-optimized Cre that produces consistent Cre activity (Koresawa et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about iCre supported by citation.

claim: tdTomato encodes a red fluorescent protein that allows cells expressing the transgene to be visualized.
source: tdTomato encodes a red fluorescent protein that allows cells expressing the transgene to be visualized (Shaner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tdTomato supported by citation.

claim: The poly A and WPRE sequences stabilize the mRNA to achieve more robust expression.
source: The poly A and WPRE sequences stabilize the mRNA to achieve more robust expression (Glover et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mRNA stabilization sequences supported by citation.

claim: tdTomato+ cells were located in the lateral, basolateral, central, and medial amygdala.
source: Immunohistochemical labeling of tdTomato in the amygdala showed that tdTomato+ cells were located in the lateral, basolateral, central, and medial amygdala (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Within the CeA, tdTomato+ cells were found to be concentrated in the CeAm, whereas the CeAl was largely devoid of tdTomato+ cells.
source: Within the CeA, tdTomato+ cells were found to be concentrated in the CeAm, whereas the CeAl was largely devoid of tdTomato+ cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: More than 90% of Crhr1-expressing cells co-express iCre in the CeAm.
source: Quantification of Crhr1- and iCre-expressing cells within the CeAm showed that more than 90% of Crhr1-expressing cells co-express iCre (Figure 2H, I).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data and quantification shown in Figures 2H and 2I.

claim: There were no significant sex differences in the number of Crhr1+, Cre+, and Crhr1+/Cre+ cells in the CeAm.
source: There were no significant sex differences in the number of Crhr1+, Cre+, and Crhr1+/Cre+ +, but there was a trend for more Crhr1+ cells in the CeAm of male rats (p = 0.07).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of cell counts from male and female rats.

claim: There was a trend for more Crhr1+ cells in the CeAm of male rats (p = 0.07).
source: There were no significant sex differences in the number of Crhr1+, Cre+, and Crhr1+/Cre+ +, but there was a trend for more Crhr1+ cells in the CeAm of male rats (p = 0.07).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of cell counts from male and female rats.

claim: The topography of CRF+ and tdTomato+ (CRF1-Cre) cells in CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats is consistent with previous studies.
source: Immunofluorescent labeling of CRF and tdTomato protein in the CeA of CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats shows that the topography of CRF+ and tdTomato+ (CRF1-Cre) cells in these rats is consistent with previous studies (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescent data shown in Figure 3 and comparison to published literature.

claim: No differences were observed between male and female membrane properties including membrane capacitance, membrane resistance, decay time constant, or resting membrane potential.
source: No differences were observed between male and female membrane properties including membrane capacitance, membrane resistance, decay time constant, or resting membrane potential (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from male and female CRF1+ CeA neurons shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The majority of CRF1+ CeA neurons were of the low-threshold bursting type.
source: The majority of CRF1+ CeA neurons were of the low-threshold bursting type (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on current clamp recordings and cell-typing analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CRF1+ neurons are under a significant amount of phasic inhibition.
source: Voltage-clamp recordings of pharmacologically-isolated GABAA receptor-mediated spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) revealed that CRF1+ neurons are under a significant amount of phasic inhibition (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is based on voltage-clamp recordings of sIPSCs shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There were no significant sex differences in sIPSC frequency or sIPSC amplitude in CRF1+ CeA neurons.
source: with no significant sex differences in sIPSC frequency (Figure 4D, left) or sIPSC amplitude (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This is based on analysis of sIPSC recordings from male and female rats shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Male and female CRF1+ CeA neurons have similar basal membrane properties and are under similar levels of basal inhibitory transmission.
source: These data indicate that male and female CRF1+ CeA neurons have similar basal membrane properties and are under similar levels of basal inhibitory transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing no sex differences.

claim: CRF1+ CeA neurons from male rats had an average baseline firing rate of 2.1 ± 0.5 Hz.
source: CRF1+ CeA neurons from male rats had an average baseline firing rate of 2.1 ± 0.5 Hz and focal application of CRF significantly increased the firing activity to 3.4 ± 0.7 Hz (t = 3.5, p = 0.011; Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This is based on cell-attached recordings from male CRF1+ CeA neurons shown in Figures 5A and 5C.

claim: Focal application of CRF significantly increased the firing activity of CRF1+ CeA neurons from male rats to 3.4 ± 0.7 Hz.
source: CRF1+ CeA neurons from male rats had an average baseline firing rate of 2.1 ± 0.5 Hz and focal application of CRF significantly increased the firing activity to 3.4 ± 0.7 Hz (t = 3.5, p = 0.011; Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This is based on cell-attached recordings from male CRF1+ CeA neurons with CRF application shown in Figures 5A and 5C.

claim: CRF1+ CeA neurons from female rats had an average baseline firing rate of 0.8 ± 0.2 Hz.
source: CRF1+ CeA neurons from female rats had an average baseline firing rate of 0.8 ± 0.2 Hz and focal application of CRF significantly increased the firing activity to 1.3 ± 0.3 Hz (t = 3.1, p = 0.016 by paired t-test; Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is based on cell-attached recordings from female CRF1+ CeA neurons shown in Figures 5B and 5D.

claim: Focal application of CRF significantly increased the firing activity of CRF1+ CeA neurons from female rats to 1.3 ± 0.3 Hz.
source: CRF1+ CeA neurons from female rats had an average baseline firing rate of 0.8 ± 0.2 Hz and focal application of CRF significantly increased the firing activity to 1.3 ± 0.3 Hz (t = 3.1, p = 0.016 by paired t-test; Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is based on cell-attached recordings from female CRF1+ CeA neurons with CRF application shown in Figures 5B and 5D.

claim: CRF application significantly increased firing in CRF1+ CeA neurons from male rats to 192.3% ± 25.6% of Control.
source: When firing activity was normalized to baseline values, CRF application significantly increased firing in CRF1+ CeA neurons from male rats to 192.3% ± 25.6% of Control (t = 3.6, p = 0.009; Figure 5E)
evidence: This is based on normalized analysis of firing rate changes in male CRF1+ CeA neurons shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CRF application significantly increased firing in CRF1+ CeA neurons from female rats to 166.5% ± 13.9% of Control.
source: and significantly increased firing in CRF1+ CeA neurons from female rats to 166.5% ± 13.9% of Control (t = 4.8, p = 0.002; Figure 5E)
evidence: This is based on normalized analysis of firing rate changes in female CRF1+ CeA neurons shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There was no significant difference in the change in firing in response to CRF between male and female CRF1+ neurons.
source: with no significant difference in the change in firing in response to CRF between male and female CRF1+ neurons.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of CRF-induced firing changes between sexes.

claim: Rats in the active virus group had a higher percentage of c-Fos+ tdTomato cells than rats in the control virus group.
source: We found that rats in the active virus group had a higher percentage of c-Fos+ tdTomato cells than rats in the control virus group (t = 7.1, p < 0.001; Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: CNO significantly increased membrane potential and number of action potentials in male CRF1+ mCitrine+ neurons in the CeA.
source: CNO (10 μM) significantly increased membrane potential and number of action potentials in both male (t = 4.3, p = 0.002; t = 2.6, p = 0.030, respectively; Figure 6C and D)
evidence: This is based on whole-cell current clamp recordings from male CRF1+ neurons expressing hM3D(Gq) shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: CNO significantly increased membrane potential and number of action potentials in female CRF1+ mCitrine+ neurons in the CeA.
source: and in female CRF1+ mCitrine+ neurons in the CeA (t = 3.2, p = 0.016; t = 3.6, p = 0.006, respectively; Figure 6E and F)
evidence: This is based on whole-cell current clamp recordings from female CRF1+ neurons expressing hM3D(Gq) shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: hM3D(Gq) receptor expression was functional and could be stimulated by CNO application with no sex differences in expression or agonist sensitivity.
source: suggesting that hM3D(Gq) receptor expression was functional and could be stimulated by CNO application with no sex differences in expression or agonist sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing CNO-induced activation in both sexes.

claim: CNO treatment decreased paw withdrawal thresholds in the Von Frey test of mechanical nociception in rats that were given intra-CeA hM3D(Gq) virus microinjections.
source: In the Von Frey test of mechanical nociception, CNO treatment decreased paw withdrawal thresholds in rats that have hM3D(Gq) expression targeted to CeA CRF1+ cells [repeated measures ANOVA; test x treatment interaction (F1,13 = 14.0, p = 0.002)].
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the Von Frey test with statistical analysis.

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases mechanical sensitivity.
source: There was a significant effect of test within the CNO group only [(F1,7 = 38.0, p < 0.001)], suggesting that chemogenetic stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Von Frey test results showing decreased paw withdrawal thresholds after CNO treatment in the hM3D(Gq) group.

claim: CNO treatment had no effect on paw withdrawal thresholds in rats that received the control EGFP fluorophore in the Von Frey test.
source: CNO treatment had no effect on paw withdrawal thresholds in rats that received the control EGFP fluorophore (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the Von Frey test in control animals shown in Figure 7C.

claim: CNO did not affect paw withdrawal latencies in either the hM3D(Gq) or control EGFP groups in the Hargreaves test of thermal nociception.
source: In the Hargreaves test of thermal nociception, CNO did not affect paw withdrawal latencies in either the hM3D(Gq) or control EGFP groups (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the Hargreaves test shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In the hM3D(Gq) group, rats that were given CNO treatment had lower open arms time compared to rats that were given vehicle treatment in the EPM test.
source: In the EPM test, in the hM3D(Gq) group, rats that were given CNO treatment had lower open arms time compared to rats that were given vehicle treatment (t-test; t = 2.6, p = 0.022)
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the EPM test with statistical analysis.

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases anxiety-like behavior on the EPM.
source: suggesting that chemogenetic stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases anxiety-like behavior on the EPM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EPM test results showing decreased open arm time after CNO treatment in the hM3D(Gq) group.

claim: Control EGFP virus rats did not show differences in open arms times after CNO treatment in the EPM test.
source: Control EGFP virus rats did not show differences in open arms times after CNO treatment (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the EPM test in control animals shown in Figure 7E.

claim: hM3D(Gq) rats that were given CNO treatment spent less time in the center of the arena compared to rats that were given vehicle treatment in the OF test.
source: In the OF field test, hM3D(Gq) rats that were given CNO treatment spent less time in the center of the arena compared to rats that were given vehicle treatment (t-test; t = 3.3, p = 0.006)
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the open field test with statistical analysis.

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases anxiety-like behavior in the OF.
source: suggesting that chemogenetic stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases anxiety-like behavior in the OF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the open field test results showing decreased center time after CNO treatment in the hM3D(Gq) group.

claim: EGFP control rats did not show differences in time spent in the center of the arena after CNO treatment in the OF test.
source: EGFP control rats did not show differences in time spent in the center of the arena after CNO treatment (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the open field test in control animals shown in Figure 7F.

claim: CNO treatment did not produce differences in time spent in the light box in either hM3D(Gq) or EGFP control groups in the LD test.
source: In the LD test, CNO treatment did not produce differences in time spent in the light box in either hM3D(Gq) or EGFP control groups (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the light-dark box test shown in Figure 7G.

claim: 98.5% of Crhr1-expressing cells co-express iCre in the BLA.
source: Quantification of Crhr1 and iCre mRNA in the BLA showed that 98.5% of Crhr1-expressing cells co-express iCre (Figure 8B, top)
evidence: This is based on RNAscope in situ hybridization data and quantification in the BLA shown in Figure 8B.

claim: 99.4% of iCre-expressing cells co-express Crhr1 in the BLA.
source: and that 99.4% of iCre-expressing cells co-express Crhr1 (Figure 8B, bottom).
evidence: This is based on RNAscope in situ hybridization data and quantification in the BLA shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Cre-tdTomato cells are found in brain areas known to contain CRF1 cells, including the prelimbic and infralimbic cortex, BNST, piriform cortex (PIR), PVN, lateral hypothalamus (LHA), paraventricular thalamus (PVT), hippocampus, ventral tegmental area (VTA), periaqueductal grey (PAG), and dorsal raphe (DR).
source: Fluorescence imaging of coronal sections across the rostrocaudal axis of CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rat brains show that Cre-tdTomato cells are found in brain areas known to contain CRF1 cells, including the prelimbic and infralimbic cortex, BNST, piriform cortex (PIR), PVN, lateral hypothalamus (LHA), paraventricular thalamus (PVT), hippocampus, ventral tegmental area (VTA), periaqueductal grey (PAG), and dorsal raphe (DR) (Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 9.

claim: A majority of cells in the BNST and PIR are tdTomato+.
source: We found that a majority of cells in the BNST and PIR, that a substantial number of cells in the PrL, IL, PVT, VTA, PAG, and DR, and that some cells in the ventral lateral septum (LSv), PVN, LHA, and hippocampus are tdTomato+.
evidence: This is based on qualitative assessment of tdTomato expression density across brain regions.

claim: A substantial number of cells in the PrL, IL, PVT, VTA, PAG, and DR are tdTomato+.
source: We found that a majority of cells in the BNST and PIR, that a substantial number of cells in the PrL, IL, PVT, VTA, PAG, and DR, and that some cells in the ventral lateral septum (LSv), PVN, LHA, and hippocampus are tdTomato+.
evidence: This is based on qualitative assessment of tdTomato expression density across brain regions.

claim: Some cells in the ventral lateral septum (LSv), PVN, LHA, and hippocampus are tdTomato+.
source: We found that a majority of cells in the BNST and PIR, that a substantial number of cells in the PrL, IL, PVT, VTA, PAG, and DR, and that some cells in the ventral lateral septum (LSv), PVN, LHA, and hippocampus are tdTomato+.
evidence: This is based on qualitative assessment of tdTomato expression density across brain regions.

claim: The lateral (LHb) and medial habenula (MHb) were largely devoid of tdTomato+ cells.
source: The lateral (LHb) and medial habenula (MHb) were largely devoid of tdTomato+ cells, but a small number of tdTomato cells were found in the ventricular zone of the MHb (Figure 9Q).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 9Q.

claim: A small number of tdTomato cells were found in the ventricular zone of the MHb.
source: The lateral (LHb) and medial habenula (MHb) were largely devoid of tdTomato+ cells, but a small number of tdTomato cells were found in the ventricular zone of the MHb (Figure 9Q).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 9Q.

claim: The locus coeruleus (LC) was devoid of tdTomato cells.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) was devoid of tdTomato cells, but a small number of tdTomato puncta was detected (Figure 9X).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 9X.

claim: A small number of tdTomato puncta was detected in the LC.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) was devoid of tdTomato cells, but a small number of tdTomato puncta was detected (Figure 9X).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 9X.

claim: tdTomato expression patterns are mostly consistent with Crhr1 mRNA expression patterns in wildtype rats.
source: These tdTomato expression patterns are mostly consistent with Crhr1 mRNA expression patterns in wildtype rats, but some species-specific differences are seen when compared to GFP expression patterns in CRF1-GFP mice.
evidence: This is based on comparison of tdTomato expression patterns with published Crhr1 mRNA data in rats and CRF1-GFP expression in mice.

claim: Some species-specific differences are seen when tdTomato expression patterns in CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats are compared to GFP expression patterns in CRF1-GFP mice.
source: These tdTomato expression patterns are mostly consistent with Crhr1 mRNA expression patterns in wildtype rats, but some species-specific differences are seen when compared to GFP expression patterns in CRF1-GFP mice.
evidence: This is based on comparison of tdTomato expression patterns with CRF1-GFP expression patterns in mice.

claim: Within the CeA of CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats, CRF1-Cre-tdTomato cells are located in the medial subdivision (CeAm).
source: We report that, within the CeA of CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats, CRF1-Cre-tdTomato cells are located in the medial subdivision (CeAm), consistent with previous reports of Crhr1 expression in rats (Potter et al., 1994; Van Pett et al., 2000; Day et al., 1999) and mice (Van Pett et al., 2000; Justice et al., 2008)
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical and in situ hybridization data from the manuscript and comparison to published literature.

claim: There is strong concordance (>90%) between Crhr1 and iCre mRNA expression in the CeAm of male and female CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats.
source: and that there is strong concordance ( > 90%) between Crhr1 and iCre mRNA expression in the CeAm of male and female CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats.
evidence: This is based on RNAscope in situ hybridization data and quantification.

claim: The basal membrane properties, inhibitory synaptic transmission, and CRF sensitivity of tdTomato-expressing CeA CRF1+ cells were characterized in male and female rats.
source: We also characterized the basal membrane properties, inhibitory synaptic transmission, and validated the CRF sensitivity of tdTomato-expressing CeA CRF1+ cells in male and female rats.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Systemic CNO treatment induces c-Fos in hM3D(Gq)-transduced CRF1+ cells in CeA.
source: that systemic CNO treatment induces c-Fos in hM3D(Gq)-transduced CRF1+ cells in CeA
evidence: This is based on c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: CNO induces membrane depolarization and spontaneous firing activity in hM3D(Gq)-transduced CRF1+ cells in CeA.
source: and that CNO induces membrane depolarization and spontaneous firing activity in hM3D(Gq)-transduced CRF1+ cells in CeA.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from hM3D(Gq)-expressing CRF1+ cells.

claim: hM3D(Gq)-mediated stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases anxiety-like behavior, as measured by EPM and open field tests.
source: We showed that hM3D(Gq)-mediated stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases anxiety-like behavior, as measured by EPM and open field tests, as well as mechanical nociception as measured by the Von Frey test.
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from EPM and open field tests.

claim: hM3D(Gq)-mediated stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases mechanical nociception as measured by the Von Frey test.
source: We showed that hM3D(Gq)-mediated stimulation of CeA CRF1+ cells increases anxiety-like behavior, as measured by EPM and open field tests, as well as mechanical nociception as measured by the Von Frey test.
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the Von Frey test.

claim: Crhr1 and iCre mRNA expression are highly colocalized in the BLA.
source: Finally, we report that Crhr1 and iCre mRNA expression are highly colocalized in the BLA
evidence: This is based on RNAscope in situ hybridization data in the BLA.

claim: Cre-tdTomato is expressed in several brain areas across the rostrocaudal axis of the rat brain in expected patterns.
source: and that Cre-tdTomato is expressed in several brain areas across the rostrocaudal axis of the rat brain in expected patterns.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging data across multiple brain regions and comparison to known CRF1 expression patterns.

claim: CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats were generated by modifying a BAC clone derived from F344 rats, that was injected into oocytes derived from Wistar rats.
source: CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats were generated by modifying a BAC clone derived from F344 rats, that was injected into oocytes derived from Wistar rats.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to generate the transgenic rat line.

claim: DNA sequence differences between F344 and Wistar rats in the 200+ kb region surrounding the Crhr1 genomic locus may impact expression of iCre-2A-tdTomato in the CRF1-Cre transgenic rat.
source: Because the originating strain of the BAC DNA differs from the strain used for transgenesis, DNA sequence differences between F344 and Wistar rats in the 200 + kb region surrounding the Crhr1 genomic locus may impact expression of iCre-2A-tdTomato in the CRF1-Cre transgenic rat.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential effects of strain differences on transgene expression.

claim: Position effect, copy number, and fragmentation of the BAC insertion may possibly alter expression of reporter genes.
source: Moreover, because transgenic BAC DNA insertion was not directed, position effect, copy number, and fragmentation of the BAC insertion may possibly alter expression of reporter genes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential effects of BAC insertion characteristics on transgene expression.

claim: Two transgenic founders were isolated that contained unique DNA sequences near the Crhr1 genomic locus in the BAC, as well as DNA sequence from both terminal ends of the injected BAC, indicating insertion of full-length BAC DNA.
source: Two transgenic founders were isolated that contained unique DNA sequences near the Crhr1 genomic locus in the BAC, as well as DNA sequence from both terminal ends of the injected BAC, indicating insertion of full-length BAC DNA.
evidence: This is based on PCR screening data of transgenic founders.

claim: One transgenic founder displayed expression of tdTomato in a pattern reflecting Crhr1 expression patterns reported in rats.
source: Of these two rats, one displayed expression of tdTomato in a pattern reflecting Crhr1 expression patterns reported in rats (Potter et al., 1994; Van Pett et al., 2000), as well as transgenic expression of reporter genes reported in similarly designed BAC transgenic mice (Justice et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2018; Hunt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison of tdTomato expression patterns with published literature.

claim: The high degree of alignment of Cre-tdTomato expression with known CRF1 expression patterns broadly throughout the brain suggests that position, copy number, or fragmentation did not substantially alter expression of the transgene.
source: However, the high degree of alignment of Cre-tdTomato expression with known CRF1 expression patterns broadly throughout the brain suggests that position, copy number, or fragmentation did not substantially alter expression of the transgene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression patterns matching known CRF1 expression.

claim: The behavioral and physiological phenotypes of CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats closely resemble those seen in wild-type Wistar rats.
source: In addition, the behavioral and physiological phenotypes of CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats reported here closely resemble those seen in wild-type Wistar rats (e.g., Itoga et al., 2016; Albrechet-Souza et al., 2020; see below), suggesting that BAC insertion did not produce observable anomalous phenotypes.
evidence: This is based on comparison of behavioral and physiological data from CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats with published data from wild-type Wistar rats.

claim: The intrinsic properties of CRF1+ (tdTomato+) CeA neurons in CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats are similar to those reported in wild-type rat CeA neurons.
source: The intrinsic properties of CRF1+ (tdTomato+) CeA neurons in CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats are similar to those reported in wild-type rat CeA neurons (Herman and Roberto, 2016), suggesting that the transgene did not significantly impact the overall health or activity of CRF1+ CeA neurons.
evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological data with published literature and inference about transgene effects.

claim: The electrophysiological properties of CRF1+ neurons in the CeA are relatively consistent between the mouse and rat transgenic models.
source: Although prior work was conducted in mouse and some species differences would be expected, the electrophysiological properties of CRF1+ neurons in the CeA are relatively consistent between the mouse and rat transgenic models.
evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological data from the current study with published data from CRFR1:GFP mice.

claim: Recent work examining sex differences in CRF1+ neurons from CRFR1:GFP mice reported similar intrinsic membrane properties, cell-typing, and baseline inhibitory transmission and noted no sex differences in basal properties between male and female CRF1+ neurons in the CeA.
source: Recent work specifically examining sex differences in CRF1+ neurons from CRFR1:GFP mice reported similar intrinsic membrane properties, cell-typing, and baseline inhibitory transmission as reported here and noted no sex differences in basal properties between male and female CRF1+ neurons in the CeA (Agoglia et al., 2020), consistent with our current findings.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: CRF was previously found to increase firing in CRF1+ CeA neurons in both male and female mice.
source: Although CRF was previously found to increase firing in CRF1+ CeA neurons in both male and female mice, CRF1+ CeA neurons from male mice displayed a significantly greater increase in firing in response to CRF application (Agoglia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: CRF1+ CeA neurons from male mice displayed a significantly greater increase in firing in response to CRF application compared to female mice.
source: Although CRF was previously found to increase firing in CRF1+ CeA neurons in both male and female mice, CRF1+ CeA neurons from male mice displayed a significantly greater increase in firing in response to CRF application (Agoglia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: The discrepancy in sex differences in CRF sensitivity between the current study and previous work may be driven by differences in sampling size, high variability in male baseline firing rates, sex differences in baseline firing rates, or it may reflect a species difference in sex-dependent sensitivity to CRF.
source: This discrepancy may be driven by differences in sampling size (although the current study was not sufficiently powered to detect sex differences), high variability in male baseline firing rates observed here, sex differences in baseline firing rates observed here, or it may reflect a species difference in sex-dependent sensitivity to CRF.
evidence: This is speculation about potential reasons for discrepancies between studies.

claim: CRF1+ neurons in the CeA have been implicated in the neuroplastic changes associated with acute and chronic ethanol exposure in mice.
source: CRF1+ neurons in the CeA have also previously been implicated in the neuroplastic changes associated with acute and chronic ethanol exposure in mice (Herman et al., 2013; Herman et al., 2016), and future work will determine if this is also the case in rats.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Pain induced by carrageenan injection into the knee joint produces hyperactivity of CeA neurons in rats, a phenomenon that is CRF1 dependent.
source: For instance, pain induced by carrageenan injection into the knee joint produces hyperactivity of CeA neurons in rats, a phenomenon that is CRF1 dependent (Ji and Neugebauer, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Latency for hind limb withdrawal reflex induced by knee joint pressure application is decreased (reflecting hyperalgesia) by CRF infusion into the CeA, a phenomenon that is blocked by co-infusion of a CRF1 antagonist.
source: Conversely, latency for hind limb withdrawal reflex induced by knee joint pressure application is decreased (reflecting hyperalgesia) by CRF infusion into the CeA, a phenomenon that is blocked by co-infusion of a CRF1 antagonist (Ji et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Ablation or inhibition of CeA CRF neurons blocks neuropathic pain-induced mechanical hypersensitivity, as measured by the Von Frey test.
source: With regard to mechanical sensitivity, our finding that DREADD activation of CeA CRF1 neurons produces mechanical hypersensitivity extends previous work showing that ablation or inhibition of CeA CRF neurons blocks neuropathic pain-induced mechanical hypersensitivity, as measured by the Von Frey test (Andreoli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: CeA CRF1 antagonism attenuates mechanical hypersensitivity produced by chronic drug or alcohol exposure.
source: Various studies have also previously reported that CeA CRF1 antagonism attenuates mechanical hypersensitivity produced by chronic drug or alcohol exposure (e.g. Cohen et al., 2015; Edwards et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Activation of CeA CRF-CRF1 signaling by chronic injuries or insults facilitates a hyperalgesic state.
source: Collectively, this prior work suggests that activation of CeA CRF-CRF1 signaling by chronic injuries or insults facilitates a hyperalgesic state, which was recapitulated in the current study via chemogenetic stimulation of CeA CRF1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on integration of previous literature and current findings.

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of CeA CRF+ cells has been shown to potentiate stress-induced analgesia.
source: It should be noted that chemogenetic stimulation of CeA CRF+ cells has been shown to potentiate stress-induced analgesia (Andreoli et al., 2017), although this effect may be due to CRF release outside the CeA (e.g. locus coeruleus) or due to changes in GABA release from CRF+ cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation, with speculation about mechanisms.

claim: Within the CeA, pharmacological studies suggest that pro- and anti-nociceptive effects of CRF signaling may be mediated by CRF1 and CRF2 receptors, respectively.
source: Within the CeA, pharmacological studies suggest that pro- and anti-nociceptive effects of CRF signaling may be mediated by CRF1 and CRF2 receptors, respectively (Ji and Neugebauer, 2007; Ji and Neugebauer, 2008), but further studies are required to delineate the precise mechanisms by which CeA CRF signaling supports hyperalgesia and analgesia.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations, with acknowledgment that further research is needed.

claim: Predator odor stress-induced hyperalgesia, as measured by the Hargreaves test, is mediated by increased CRF-CRF1 signaling in the CeA.
source: Our lab has shown that predator odor stress-induced hyperalgesia, as measured by the Hargreaves test, is mediated by increased CRF-CRF1 signaling in the CeA (Itoga et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study by the authors' lab supported by citation.

claim: Specific CeA cell populations may be involved in specific types of nociceptive processing.
source: It is possible that specific CeA cell populations are involved in specific types of nociceptive processing, or it is possible that the engagement/recruitment of CeA CRF1+ cells in mediating specific types of nociception depends on the animal's history or affective state.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying differential nociceptive responses.

claim: The engagement/recruitment of CeA CRF1+ cells in mediating specific types of nociception may depend on the animal's history or affective state.
source: It is possible that specific CeA cell populations are involved in specific types of nociceptive processing, or it is possible that the engagement/recruitment of CeA CRF1+ cells in mediating specific types of nociception depends on the animal's history or affective state.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying differential nociceptive responses.

claim: In mice, intra-CeA infusion of a CRF1 antagonist attenuates anxiety-like behavior, as measured by open field and light-dark box tests, following immobilization stress but not under basal conditions.
source: For instance, in mice, intra-CeA infusion of a CRF1 antagonist attenuates anxiety-like behavior, as measured by open field and light-dark box tests, following immobilization stress but not under basal conditions (Henry et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Blockade of CRF-CRF1 signaling in the CeA attenuates alcohol withdrawal-induced anxiety in rats, as measured by the EPM test.
source: Similarly, blockade of CRF-CRF1 signaling in the CeA attenuates alcohol withdrawal-induced anxiety in rats, as measured by the EPM test (Rassnick et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Exposure to stressors increases extracellular CRF levels in the CeA.
source: Exposure to stressors (Merlo Pich et al., 1995) and alcohol withdrawal (Zorrilla et al., 2001) both increase extracellular CRF levels in the CeA.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Alcohol withdrawal increases extracellular CRF levels in the CeA.
source: Exposure to stressors (Merlo Pich et al., 1995) and alcohol withdrawal (Zorrilla et al., 2001) both increase extracellular CRF levels in the CeA.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: CeA CRF cell activation (using DREADDs) increases anxiety-like behavior and this effect is blocked by CeA CRF knockdown using RNA interference.
source: Messing and colleagues used CRF-Cre rats to show that CeA CRF cell activation (using DREADDs) increases anxiety-like behavior and that this effect is blocked by CeA CRF knockdown using RNA interference (Pomrenze et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Increased CRF-CRF1 signaling in CeA, whether produced by stress exposure, drug withdrawal, or the use of viral genetic tools, supports anxiogenesis.
source: Collectively, these studies show that increased CRF-CRF1 signaling in CeA, whether produced by stress exposure, drug withdrawal, or the use of viral genetic tools, supports anxiogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on integration of multiple previous studies and current findings.

claim: The light-dark box test may be more suited for detecting anxiolytic rather than anxiogenic effects.
source: Previous studies reported that the light-dark box test may be more suited for detecting anxiolytic rather than anxiogenic effects (Crawley and Davis, 1982), and that animals' responses in this test is affected by the intensity of illumination in the animal's regular housing room (File et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Animals' responses in the light-dark box test are affected by the intensity of illumination in the animal's regular housing room.
source: Previous studies reported that the light-dark box test may be more suited for detecting anxiolytic rather than anxiogenic effects (Crawley and Davis, 1982), and that animals' responses in this test is affected by the intensity of illumination in the animal's regular housing room (File et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Female rats in proestrus have higher levels of CeA Crf mRNA than male rats.
source: For example, female rats in proestrus have higher levels of CeA Crf mRNA than male rats and footshock stress induces greater CeA Crf expression in female proestrus than in male rats (Iwasaki-Sekino et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Footshock stress induces greater CeA Crf expression in female proestrus than in male rats.
source: For example, female rats in proestrus have higher levels of CeA Crf mRNA than male rats and footshock stress induces greater CeA Crf expression in female proestrus than in male rats (Iwasaki-Sekino et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Using autoradiography, there were no sex differences in CRF1 receptor binding in the CeA of rats.
source: However, using autoradiography, Cooke and colleagues reported no sex differences in CRF1 receptor binding in the CeA of rats (Weathington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Using a transgenic CRFR1:GFP mouse line, the CeA of male animals was shown to contain more CRF1+ cells than female animals.
source: Using a transgenic CRFR1:GFP mouse line, the CeA of male animals was shown to contain more CRF1+ cells than female animals (Agoglia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study supported by citation.

claim: Male CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats tend to have more CRF1+ cells within the CeA than female rats, as detected via RNAscope in situ hybridization.
source: In the current study, although underpowered to detect sex effects, we found that male CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rats tend to have more CRF1+ cells within the CeA than female rats, as detected via RNAscope in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is based on RNAscope in situ hybridization data from the current study.

claim: The anxiogenic effect of CeA CRF1+ cell activation in the EPM test was driven by stronger effects in male subjects.
source: However, we observed that the anxiogenic effect of CeA CRF1+ cell activation in the EPM test was driven by stronger effects in male subjects.
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the EPM test showing sex-specific effects.

claim: CeA CRF1+ cell activation may affect specific components of anxiety-related behavior, and these components are aligned with specific 'anxiety-like behavior' phenotypes in male versus female rats that are more or less detectable by various tests.
source: One interpretation is that CeA CRF1+ cell activation affects specific components of anxiety-related behavior, that these components are aligned with specific 'anxiety-like behavior' phenotypes in male versus female rats that are more or less detectable by these various tests.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying sex differences in behavioral responses.

claim: A meta-analysis of studies of anxiety-like behavior in rats and mice revealed a discordance in results between the EPM and open field tests.
source: In support of this idea, a meta-analysis of studies of anxiety-like behavior in rats and mice revealed a discordance in results between the EPM and open field tests (Mohammad et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous meta-analysis supported by citation.

claim: Studies have shown that the EPM test is more reliable for detecting anxiogenic effects in male rather than female rodents.
source: Within the EPM literature, studies have shown that the EPM test is more reliable for detecting anxiogenic effects in male rather than female rodents (e.g. Scholl et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citation.

claim: The CRF1-Cre rat can be used to study the role of distinct CRF1+ cell populations and circuits in physiology and behavior.
source: In summary, we present a novel CRF1-Cre-tdTomato rat line that allows for the visualization and manipulation of CRF1-expressing cells. The CRF1-Cre rat can be used to study the role of distinct CRF1+ cell populations and circuits in physiology and behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the new transgenic rat line based on the validation data presented.

claim: The expression of the fluorescent reporter tdTomato in CRF1-expressing cells will allow for high resolution, detailed analysis of the expression pattern of CRF1 that has not been possible due to the lack of CRF1-specific antibodies.
source: In addition, the expression of the fluorescent reporter tdTomato in CRF1-expressing cells will allow for high resolution, detailed analysis of the expression pattern of CRF1 that has not been possible due to the lack of CRF1-specific antibodies.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the tdTomato reporter for anatomical studies.
